text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Wages in Sweden are forecast to rise by six percent in 1997 while the average rise across in Europe will be 3.2 percent, according to the Edin group, a committee appointed by the government to investigate wages.

- Russian paper Nezavisimaja Gazeta reported in its last 1996 issue that Swedish intelligence through an advisor in the Baltic countries attempted to enlist Russian agents to shed some light on alleged foreign submarine trespassing in Swedish waters. According to the paper, Swedes have enticed a Russian contact with large sums of money and promises of right of abode in Sweden if in trouble. But the agent, a marine officer at the Russian base Baltijsk in Kaliningrad, fooled the Swedes and disclosed all to the domestic secret service FSB.
- Different election days for municipal and government elections are necessary as the established party groups are not appropriate, acccording to professor Benny Hjern in Gothenburg.

- The government wants to abolish the right to appeal a sentence given in a district court to a higher court. The higher court will merely take on cases that have been given a special appeal right which only will be given under certain circumstances.
- A four-month upturn for Swedish industries slowed in December with Swedbank and Silf's purchasing managers' index showing unchanged activity in December compared with November.

- Banking group Handelsbanken and brokerage Hagstromer & Qviberg are the only two among the ten largest brokers in Sweden that increased their market shares in 1996, Stockholm Stock Exchange statistics showed. Handelsbanken has reached a 13 percent market share, up from 10 percent, thereby pushing rival S-E-Banken off its position as the largest player on the bourse.

- Newspaper sources say the Swedish state is selling 20-25 percent of its stake in Nordbanken to the Wallenberg empire's investment arm, Investor AB. The sale, costing 7.5-9.5 billion crowns according to the paper, paves the way for a merger between Nordbanken and S-E-Banken in which the Wallenberg family has a large presence.
- Companies are expecting the new company car rules to boost buying of cars in 1997 with sales for the first part of the year getting off to a flying start.
- The number of companies in the ski resort Are, the largest in Scandinavia, has risen steadily in the past few years. These are mainly concentrated in media and information technology.
